source.title: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Internal Representation Unlearning for Large Language Models
source.authors: Tomoya Yamashita; Akira Ito; Yuuki Yamanaka; Masanori Yamada; Takayuki Miura; Toshiki Shibahara

record.tranche_reason: The study compares unlearning methods and analyzes their effects on internal representations. Its results argue that suppression-based methods can reduce output scores while leaving target-related activation information largely intact, and that the proposed representation-level method changes those activations.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates FB, QA, and adversarial-attack (AA) probes after unlearning. AA includes jailbreak-style prompts, including cross-lingual queries. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning or quantization, or by ablating an activation direction. The AA scores are not a matched comparison of ordinary and adversarial prompts, and there is no model that never learned the target knowledge. Main-table rows below use the reported aggregate forget score and AA score; FB and QA sub-scores and additional per-epoch and figure results are not all included.
record.test_reason: The study's own results bear on two versions. Section 4.3 measures GA-unlearned Llama3.1-8B at the checkpoint where forget score reaches 0% and finds the attribute rate virtually unchanged and known-entity latents still active, which is direct evidence for C (suppression rather than deletion). Table 1 gives forget, AA, retain and utility scores for GA, NPO, RMU and the proposed method on two models, bearing on A, and on E and F through the RWKU jailbreak-style AA probes. None of the three original sources is this study.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that their SAE recognition-latent method gives the lowest forget scores while preserving retain and utility, and that it removes target information from internal representations. They say suppression-based baselines cannot do this even when their output forget score reaches 0%. They add that baselines' retain and utility look intact in Table 1 only because of early stopping. They admit their method does not reach a forget score of zero.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a different SAE-guided recognition-latent method and compares it with GA, NPO, and RMU; it does not reproduce the cited unlearning studies' recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary by model and by unlearning input format (sentence, entity name, or last token). The evaluation also separates FB, QA, and AA probes; the study does not provide matched prompts to isolate the effect of adversarial prompting.
record.problems: The study has no never-trained or oracle-model comparison for the recovery question and states no chance-level benchmark. The internal-representation results are partly figure-based, without numeric values in the text. AA uses a different probe format from QA, so the reported results do not isolate the causal effect of jailbreak or rephrasing prompts. The main experiment covers two instruction-tuned models and 100 target entities.
record.rows_left_out: The table's separate FB and QA scores, other utility axes, per-epoch curves, and additional appendix figures for NPO, RMU, and Gemma were not extracted as separate rows. The main table already records aggregate forget and AA results for each method and model; the omitted results are in Table 1, Appendix A, and Figures 4–16.

untested.parts: No relearning or fine-tuning recovery attack.
No ablation or edit of an activation direction to restore answers. Evidence is from logit-lens attribute rate and SAE latent proxies only.
The nine AA prompt types (prefix injection, role-play, synonym, cross-lingual) are not reported separately. There is no in-context information attack and no item-matched non-attack comparison.
The proposed method is not tested against fine-tuning, ablation or quantization attacks.
No oracle or never-trained model and no chance reference. Utility is reported on only two of six axes in the rows.

missing.what: Separate QA (and FB) forget scores per method and model, needed as the within-model baseline for judging AA elicitation under E. My E verdicts use these Table 1 values.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Table 1, FB and QA columns

missing.what: Attribute-rate and recognition-latent results for NPO and RMU baselines and for Gemma2-9B. These are figure-only and the text gives no description of the trends.
Remaining utility axes for the proposed method (e.g. Gemma BBH 30.4 vs 33.9, Fluency 635.5 vs 644.7)

record.verdict_notes: The AA-vs-QA comparison is my derivation from Table 1; RWKU AA and QA probes are not item-matched, so E verdicts are cautious. Section 4.3 uses a different checkpoint (forget score reaching 0%) from Table 1. The paper text says 'Llama3.1-9B' there, which is a typo for Llama3.1-8B. No uncertainty is reported, and Table 1 covers 100 of the 200 RWKU entities.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports forget scores and retain and utility measures, but does not establish a chance-level reference. It does not compare attacked unlearned models with models that never learned the target.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery attack.
No activation-direction ablation or test of whether ablation restores target knowledge. The study analyzes activation proxies, not direct recovery of target answers by an internal edit.

The study tests AA prompts, including jailbreak-style and cross-lingual prompts, but does not isolate rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information as separate attacks, nor compare each attack with a matched non-attack prompt.
The proposed method is evaluated on AA probes, but the study does not test whether it resists fine-tuning, activation ablation, or quantization recovery attacks.
